title: Dying Business or Generational Opportunity? FICO's drop explained.
creator: Brian Feroldi
summary: Brian Feroldi asks whether Fair Isaac (FICO) is a dying business or a generational opportunity after a fall of about 66% from its all-time high. He explains FICO's two segments: credit scores, about two-thirds of revenue, and bank software for account opening, fraud and marketing, about one-third. Revenue was about $2.4 billion over the last 12 months, roughly 90% from the Americas, with over $1 billion of operating cash flow and no dividend — a phase-four, capital-return business. He calls the moat wide: software lock-in, the FICO score as a de facto regulatory standard, a very strong brand and 54% returns on capital. Growth has not collapsed: revenue rose more than 20% and earnings 25% over the last year, analysts expect about 28% revenue growth in 2027, and management raised full-year 2026 guidance. He gives three reasons for the fall. First, aggressive mortgage-score pricing — from about 60 cents to $10 since 2022 — angered lenders, drew monopoly criticism and pushed Rocket Mortgage toward VantageScore. Second, a September 2026 move by the FHFA's Bill Pulte put FICO and VantageScore on one pricing grid, removing FICO's government preference; VantageScore is offered at 99 cents. Third, FICO borrowed heavily for $2.3 billion of buybacks, likely above 30 times earnings. At about 23 times earnings versus a 10-year average near 50 times, Feroldi leans opportunity over trap, but says the damaged moat means he wants an even cheaper valuation before getting excited. Call: FICO — CONDITIONAL_BUY, first tracked, no dollar price stated.

calls.thesis: First tracked Feroldi FICO call: leans opportunity over value trap, but wants an even cheaper valuation than today before getting excited — stock down ~66% from its all-time high at ~23x earnings (vs ~50x 10-year average), revenue +20%+ and earnings +25% over the last year with 2027 revenue growth expected ~28% and full-year 2026 guidance raised, wide moat (54% return on capital, software lock-in, de facto standard score) now damaged by egregious mortgage-score price rises (60c to $10 since 2022), Rocket Mortgage switching preference to VantageScore, and a September 2026 FHFA move to one pricing grid giving VantageScore equal terms (Vantage offered at 99c vs FICO $10); third concern is $2.3B of debt-funded buybacks done likely above 30x earnings while the shares were in freefall. Opportunity only if no more share loss, growth persists and buybacks prove well-timed; a trap if the monopoly is gone for good.
calls.price_at_call: Down ~66% from all-time high; trading at ~23x earnings (no dollar share price stated)
